analysis.one_liner: Lets investors fund students' education in exchange for a share of their future income.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to three House committees and later to a subcommittee, but no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a legal framework for "income share agreements" — contracts in which an investor pays for a student's education and the student repays a set percentage of future earnings for up to 30 years. It would make these contracts enforceable nationwide, override state usury laws and state rules on wage assignments, make the obligations non-dischargeable in bankruptcy, give the money favorable tax treatment, and exempt the businesses making these agreements from investment-company regulation. It sets some limits: at least the first $10,000 of income is exempt, no one can commit more than 15% of future income, and payment terms and disclosures are required. The bill never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, students who need money for college or job training but want payments that adjust with their income could have used income share agreements instead of traditional loans, with the first $10,000 of income shielded and no more than 15% of income committed. Investors and financial firms would have gained a new, federally sanctioned product: their contracts would be enforceable nationwide, exempt from state interest-rate caps, immune from bankruptcy discharge by the student, and free of investment-company regulation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: ISA investors, and some students seeking flexible funding

how_it_helps.text: It makes income share agreements valid, enforceable contracts nationwide, giving students a way to pay for school that adjusts with their income — payments fall in bad years and rise in good ones.

It builds in some student protections: at least the first $10,000 of income each year (adjusted for inflation) is exempt, no one can commit more than 15% of future income, and the payment period generally cannot exceed 30 years.
Money received under an income share agreement would not count as income or assets when calculating federal financial aid, and would be excluded from taxable income, like a loan.

analysis.who_pays: Students whose careers pay well would repay far more than they received, and they could not wipe out the obligation in bankruptcy. States would lose their authority to cap interest or restrict the sale of future wages under these contracts.

drawbacks.text: Obligations under an income share agreement would not be dischargeable in bankruptcy, a protection available to most student borrowers with federal loans and to ordinary debtors.
The bill overrides state usury laws and state laws regulating assignments of future wages, removing state-level consumer protections from these contracts.

The bill caps the share of income (15%) and the payment period (30 years) but sets no cap on the total dollar amount a student could end up repaying relative to what they received, so high earners could pay many multiples of the funds they got.
Businesses making income share agreements would be excluded from the Investment Company Act of 1940, removing a layer of federal investment-company oversight from the funds behind these contracts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real flexibility: students could fund school without taking on fixed debt, and payments would fall if their income fell. But the protections were thin relative to the risk. It made obligations non-dischargeable in bankruptcy, stripped away state usury laws, exempted the funds from investment-company regulation, and put no ceiling on the total dollar amount a student could end up paying — only a percentage and a time limit. A student who earns well could repay far more than they received, with no way out through bankruptcy. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill was built more for investors than for students.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees, then sent to a subcommittee in June 2014, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Petri introduced the bill on April 9, 2014.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Financial Services Committees the day it was introduced.
On June 13, 2014, it was referred to the Higher Education and Workforce Training Subcommittee; no committee vote, floor vote, or further action followed.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State usury laws, state rules on wage assignments, and standard bankruptcy protections remained fully intact, and no new federally preempted market for claims on students' future income was created. The private education-finance industry gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State consumer-protection rules and standard bankruptcy rights

for.name: Rep. Thomas E. Petri
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, and Financial Services Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral the day it was introduced and never reported it out; no committee vote was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans sponsored and cosponsored the bill, but no recorded vote ever showed where the parties stood, and no opposition was recorded.

industries.industry: Private education finance and ISA investors
industries.note: The bill creates the legal foundation for a new industry: investors who fund students in exchange for a share of future earnings, freed from state usury caps, bankruptcy risk, and investment-company regulation. The industry's revenue comes directly out of students' future paychecks.
Income share agreements would compete with conventional student loans, though the bill also legitimizes and expands the private education-financing market overall.

A new private payment channel could bring tuition dollars from students who cannot or will not borrow conventionally. The bill also keeps ISA money from counting against students in federal aid formulas, preserving their other aid.
